samasa.sense: his kingdom freed of the enemies who had taken it (1.5–8)

morph.note: Perfect of √वृ ‘to choose’ in the ātmanepada: reduplicated व-, root vowel ṛ becomes r before the vowel ending: व-व्र्-ए. ‘He chose (for himself)’.
Neuter accusative of an -इन् stem: विभ्रंशिन् (वि + √भ्रंश् + -इन्, ‘apt to fall away’) loses its n in the neuter nominative/accusative singular.
Ablative used as an adverb: ‘by force’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः नृपः अन्यजन्मनि अविभ्रंशि राज्यम्, अत्र एव च बलात् हतशत्रुबलं निजं राज्यं वव्रे।
mantras.anvaya_en: One verb (वव्रे) with two objects, each a kingdom: one ‘in another birth’, one ‘here itself’, joined by च.
mantras.lit: Then the king chose an imperishable kingdom in another birth, and here itself his own kingdom, its enemies’ forces destroyed by force.
mantras.tr: Then the king chose a kingdom that would never be lost, in another life — and, in this very life, his own kingdom back, his enemies’ power broken by force.

comm.t: The king’s choice is double: a lasting sovereignty in a future birth, and the return of his own kingdom now. Both are worldly; he asks for the restoration of what was lost and for more than he had.

Suratha’s request is read as the choice of bhoga, enjoyment — the first of the gifts Medhas named in 13.5 (भोगस्वर्गापवर्गदा). The Goddess grants it without reproach; the text does not judge the choice.

samasa.literal: he whose mind is weary (of the world)
samasa.sense: the merchant, disillusioned with the family and wealth that had cast him out

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (with a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa as its first member)
samasa.literal: the maker of the falling-away of attachment
samasa.sense: knowledge that loosens the bond of attachment

morph.note: ‘Mine’ and ‘I’ (मम … अहम्) are quoted words, each closed by इति. They name the two forms of attachment from which the knowledge releases: ownership (ममता, cf. 1.53 ममतावर्त्ते) and the ego-sense (अहंता).
कारक is an agent noun in -अक (ण्वुल्) from √कृ: ‘one that makes’. It agrees with ज्ञानम् (n. acc. sg.).

mantras.anvaya: ततः निर्विण्णमानसः प्राज्ञः सः वैश्यः अपि ‘मम’ इति ‘अहम्’ इति सङ्गविच्युतिकारकं ज्ञानं वव्रे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject with three qualifiers, verb and object. The quoted words ‘मम’ इति ‘अहम्’ इति define the attachment (सङ्ग) that the knowledge removes.
mantras.lit: That merchant too, then, his mind disenchanted, the wise one, chose knowledge that brings about the falling-away of attachment (expressed as) ‘mine’ and ‘I’.
mantras.tr: The merchant, his heart turned from the world, wisely chose knowledge — the knowledge that frees one from the attachment of ‘mine’ and ‘I’.
mantras.tr_note: The epithet प्राज्ञः (‘the wise one’) is rendered adverbially (‘wisely’).

comm.t: The merchant chooses the other gift: knowledge that releases attachment. The text names that attachment precisely — the thoughts ‘mine’ and ‘I’. It was this that had kept both men bound to people and things they knew had wronged them (1.41–45).

The tradition reads the merchant’s choice as apavarga, liberation — the last of the gifts in 13.5. The two men, who came to the seer with the same affliction, leave with the two great goals: enjoyment and release.
A modern reading: the merchant had more reason than the king to ask for his property back. He asks instead to be free of needing it.

sandhi.note: Visarga after ai and i, before a vowel or a voiced consonant, is sounded as r.
Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra.

samasa.type: prādi tatpuruṣa (सु as an intensifying first member)

morph.note: Future of प्र + √आप्. The root is parasmaipada (प्राप्स्यति), and a passive would not fit (भवान् is the agent and राज्यम् the object). The ātmanepada ending is a licence of Epic and Purāṇic verse.
अहन् ‘day’: before consonantal case endings its final n is replaced by ru (a special rule for this word), which becomes u after a: अह + u + भिः → अहोभिः. Compare अहः (nom.) and अहानि (nom. pl.).
भवत् is the respectful ‘you’; grammatically a third-person noun, so its verb is third person (प्राप्स्यते, भविष्यति).

mantras.anvaya: नृपते, भवान् स्वल्पैः अहोभिः स्वं राज्यं प्राप्स्यते।
mantras.anvaya_en: A simple sentence: vocative, subject (honorific भवान्), time (instrumental), object, verb.
mantras.lit: In very few days, O king, you will obtain your own kingdom.
mantras.tr: Within a few days, O king, you will regain your own kingdom.
mantras.tr_note: प्राप्स्यते ‘will obtain’ is rendered ‘will regain’, since the kingdom is his own (स्वम्).

comm.t: The first boon is granted with a time: ‘in a few days’. The king’s wish for the kingdom ‘here itself’ (13.17) is answered first.

sandhi.note: Final n after a long vowel is not doubled before a vowel; it simply joins the a. The final m becomes anusvāra before t.

morph.note: Absolutive of √हन् (the nasal is lost before -त्वा). Its agent is the king, who here appears only in the genitive तव: a loose but common construction in Purāṇic verse.
A neuter participle used as an abstract noun or with राज्यम् understood from 13.20: ‘your (rule) will be unshaken’.

mantras.anvaya: (त्वं) रिपून् हत्वा, तत्र तव (राज्यम्) अस्खलितं भविष्यति।
mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive phrase (हत्वा रिपून्) and a main clause whose subject is अस्खलितम्, with राज्यम् understood from 13.20.
mantras.lit: Having slain the enemies, yours there will be unshaken.
mantras.tr: You will slay your enemies, and your rule there will stand unshaken.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Rule’ is supplied for the substantive neuter अस्खलितम् (‘what is unshaken’); the absolutive is rendered as a coordinate verb.

comm.t: The second part of the first boon: the enemies who took the kingdom will be slain, and the king’s rule will be secure. The ‘enemies’ force destroyed’ that he asked for (हतशत्रुबलम्, 13.17) is promised.
